beats.intro: Learning module eight. [[sub]]What an option is worth before maturity, and what drives that value.
beats.exercise: [[head]]Before maturity, ask: what would the option be worth if it could be exercised now? That is its exercise value. [[call]]For a call, it is the spot price minus the present value of the exercise price, or zero if that is negative. [[put]]For a put, it is the present value of the exercise price minus the spot price, or zero. [[ex]]Take a one-year put with an exercise price of one thousand euros, and a one percent rate. Six months in, the spot price is nine hundred fifty. [[calc]]The present value of one thousand for six months is nine ninety-five oh four. So the exercise value is forty-five euros oh four.
beats.money: [[head]]Moneyness compares the spot price with the exercise price. [[call]]A call is in the money when the spot price is above X, at the money when they are equal, and out of the money when the spot is below. [[put]]For a put, it is the reverse: in the money when the spot is below X. Our put, with the spot at nine fifty, is fifty euros in the money. [[deep]]Moneyness also drives sensitivity. A deep in-the-money option moves almost one for one with the underlying. A deep out-of-the-money option barely moves. And near the money, small moves decide whether it will be exercised.
beats.timevalue: [[eq]]An option's price is its exercise value plus its time value. [[ex]]If our put trades at fifty euros, and its exercise value is forty-five oh four, its time value is four euros ninety-six. [[why]]Time value reflects the chance that the price moves favorably before maturity. More time, or more volatility, means more possible outcomes. [[decay]]Time value is always positive, and it shrinks to zero at maturity. This is time value decay.
beats.bounds: [[head]]Arbitrage sets bounds on option prices. [[clow]]A call can never be worth less than its exercise value: the spot price minus the present value of X, or zero. [[cup]]And no one pays more than the underlying itself for the right to buy it. So the call's upper bound is the spot price. [[ex]]Example: a one-year call with X of one thousand euros, one percent rate. Six months in, the spot is one thousand fifty. [[exans]]The lower bound is one thousand fifty minus nine ninety-five oh four: fifty-four ninety-six. The upper bound is one thousand fifty. [[put]]For a put, the lower bound is the present value of X minus the spot price, or zero. And the upper bound is X itself.
beats.replicate: [[call]]Can we replicate an option, like a forward? A call rises with the underlying, like a long forward, but only pays when it is exercised. [[fwd]]For a forward, we borrow the present value of the forward price and buy the asset, and hold that until maturity. [[part]]For a call, exercise is uncertain. So we borrow only a fraction of the present value of X, and buy a fraction of the underlying, based on the likelihood of exercise. [[put]]A put is replicated the other way: short the underlying and lend. [[adjust]]And because the likelihood of exercise keeps changing, an option's replicating position must be adjusted over time. A forward's never changes.
beats.underlying: [[head]]Now the factors that drive an option's value. [[s]]First, the underlying price. A higher price raises a call's value and lowers a put's, just like long and short forwards. [[sens]]But the effect is not one for one. It is stronger the more likely the option is to be exercised. [[x]]Second, the exercise price. A lower X makes a call more valuable: more likely to be exercised, and paying more when it is. [[xp]]A higher X makes a put more valuable.
beats.others: [[t]]Third, time to expiration. More time raises a call's value: the upside is unlimited, the downside capped at the premium. [[tp]]For a put it usually helps too, but not always: a deep in-the-money put waits longer to collect its payoff, which lowers its present value. [[r]]Fourth, the risk-free rate. A higher rate lowers the present value of X. That raises a call's value, and lowers a put's. [[vol]]Fifth, volatility. A wider range of possible prices raises the chance of a big payoff, while the loss is still capped. Higher volatility raises the value of both calls and puts.
beats.carry: [[inc]]Last, income and costs of owning the underlying. Income, such as dividends or a convenience yield, goes to the owner of the asset, not the option holder. It lowers a call's value and raises a put's. [[cost]]Carrying costs, such as storage, do the opposite. [[table]]Here is the full picture. An increase in each factor, and its effect on calls and puts.
beats.wrap: [[w1]]Exercise value compares the spot price with the present value of the exercise price. [[w2]]Option price equals exercise value plus time value, which decays to zero at maturity. [[w3]]Arbitrage bounds: a call lies between its exercise value and the spot price; a put between its exercise value and X. [[w4]]Volatility and time raise option values; the underlying, exercise price, rate and income push calls and puts in opposite directions.
beats.finish: That's the end of learning module eight.
